answer:
Enron staff did not say much about megawatt laundering in their own words. The phrase appears in only 15 emails (mail_counts), from 2000-10-30 to 2001-11-26, and everything I read was forwarded press or a circulated clipping with no Enron comment. The senders were Enron's media and regulatory staff (Miyung Buster, Ann Schmidt, Alan Comnes), a Bracewell & Patterson lawyer, and a lobbying firm. I did not read the two McNally Temple emails or the Kaminski AOL email. So this shows what Enron circulated, not what its people thought.

What those clippings said:
- **Oct 2000, via Bracewell & Patterson.** A San Jose Mercury News piece described "megawatt laundering" as a possible multi-company conspiracy to evade California's wholesale price cap, which covers power generated in California but not power sold in from elsewhere. An industry chairman said there was no evidence it was occurring and called it "an urban legend." A Stanford economist said the ISO's market surveillance committee had warned of the potential in at least two reports.
- **Mar 2001, forwarded by Alan Comnes.** A draft ISO export-ban proposal said a ban could help prevent generators from selling power out of state to an affiliate or associate and then back into California just before it was needed.
- **Apr–Jun 2001.** A New York Times piece (Apr 27) said FERC's new order included a provision meant to discourage the practice, but California officials were skeptical. An ISO filing said the new plan still failed "to take any constructive steps to eliminate or even to minimize the pernicious effects of 'megawatt laundering.'" That quote is in a June 2001 press digest circulated at Enron.
- **Sep 2001.** A press item in a "CA Issues" clipping said tougher federal rules enacted in May and June appeared to be curtailing "megawatt laundering" schemes.
- **Nov 2001, forwarded by Alan Comnes during the Dynegy merger review.** The article quoted Lt. Gov. Bustamante's lawsuit against the "Big Five" generators, alleging they "engaged in 'megawatt laundering,' in which they made trades with the primary purpose of inflating the costs of electricity." That suit named Dynegy, Williams, Mirant, Reliant and Duke, not Enron.

I found no Enron-authored email that defends, denies or explains the practice. The one Enron-authored comment near the topic is Steve Hall's March 2001 note that California was building "a one-way wall around the state" and that "like the roach motel, megawatts check into California, but they don't check out." It is about export curtailment, not laundering, and doesn't use the term.

Other wordings I searched, such as "Ricochet" and re-importing power to avoid the cap, found no Enron discussion of such trades. My searches may have missed some, so I can't rule it out.

The price-control feature of the new FERC plan covers more hours than the 
previous one but will still be restricted to times of relatively tight 
supply. Critics say controls should be in effect during all hours, since 
prices have often been high around the clock. 
Plus, the new plan still fails "to take any constructive steps to eliminate 
or even to minimize the pernicious effects of `megawatt laundering,'" says a

the latest plan, which leaves suppliers with a large potential loophole for

Energy conservation efforts leave California blackouts in the dark 
State has reported no shutdowns since May 
By JOHN WOOLFOLK 
Knight Ridder News Service 
Tuesday, September 4, 2001 
San Jose, Calif. -- This was supposed to be California 's summer of darkness, but as the summer draws to a close without any blackouts, the doomsayers are proving to be wrong. 
Just a few months ago, they talked about 20 hours of rolling blackouts. Or 250 hours. Even 1,000 hours. But the blackouts stopped in early May. 
Mild weather and surprisingly strong consumer conservation saved the day, with help from new power plants and market controls. Consider: 
-- State officials had hoped to lower peak power demand by 2,300 megawatts -- about equal to a nuclear power plant -- with a $600 million effort to promote conservation and efficiency. Consumers saved as much as 5,500 megawatts. 
-- Average temperatures were above normal in June, but not as high as last year, and cooler than normal in July and August. More important, there haven't been the severe regional heat waves that strain the power grid. 
-- Six new power plants have gone online so far this summer, totaling more than 1,600 megawatts. The three largest, accounting for 1,400 megawatts, had been in the works for years. The others were rushed into production under a state effort to boost peak supplies. 
-- Tougher federal regulations enacted in May and June prohibit California power plant owners from withholding power from the grid in emergencies and appear to be curtailing "megawatt laundering" schemes. 
Which played the greatest role may be debated for years. But even if it was mostly just good weather, Gov. Gray Davis is praising Californians. 
Davis had initially urged consumers to cut back 8%, then upped it to 10% and offered 20% rebates to those who conserved 20% over last year.

The ISO argued that under its tariff it has the authority to cut schedules in 
emergency situations.  True.  But the reality is that the "emergency" is 
self-inflicted; by imposing price caps (another part of this Market 
Stabilization plan), the ISO is driving supply out of California.  As others 
have argued, the only "emergency" is price:  California has made a decision 
to keep consumer rates artificially low, and its use of price-controls has 
reduced the supply---causing a supply "emergency"---, and the ISO now seeks 
to increase its supply by building a one-way wall around the state of 
California.  Like the roach motel, megawatts check into California, but they 
don't check out.
